brief.scenario: Ms Rachel Linford, 42, had triple assessment for a lump in her left breast last week. The core biopsy shows invasive breast cancer (no special type, grade 2), oestrogen receptor positive and HER2 negative. Imaging shows an 18 mm tumour; axillary ultrasound is normal. The MDT recommends surgery first. Sarah, the breast care nurse, is with you.
brief.task: Give Ms Linford her result and discuss the next steps.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Find out what she knows, warn, say "cancer", stop. Then the plan, in her order.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Filling the silence after the word "cancer" with treatment details she cannot take in.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "What's been going through your mind since the biopsy last week?"

flow: Set up and find out what she knows

grid.label: Setting and her perception
grid.fail: Starts with the result without checking who she wants present or what she expects.
grid.pass: Introduces self and nurse, confirms identity, checks whether she wants anyone with her, asks what she knows.
grid.high: Asks how much detail she would like today before giving the result.

grid.label: Warning shot and diagnosis
grid.fail: Uses euphemism ("abnormal cells", "a growth") or jargon, and never says "cancer".
grid.pass: Gives a warning shot, then says plainly that the biopsy shows breast cancer.
grid.high: Stops after the word "cancer" and waits for her to speak first.

grid.label: Responding to emotion
grid.fail: Carries on with the plan while she is crying, or offers false reassurance.
grid.pass: Acknowledges her distress, allows silence, offers time and a tissue.
grid.high: Names the emotion and asks what is worrying her most before giving more information.

grid.label: What the result means
grid.fail: Cannot explain the result, or guesses at prognosis or cure.
grid.pass: Explains in plain words: found early, small, no sign of spread to the armpit on scan, treatable with the aim of cure.
grid.high: Explains hormone-sensitive: tablets that block oestrogen will be part of treatment; honest that the operation gives final staging.

grid.label: Next steps
grid.fail: Gives no plan, or promises a specific operation or outcome.
grid.pass: Surgery first: removing the lump with a lymph node check under the arm, or removing the breast; the surgeon will discuss both.
grid.high: Explains similar survival for either operation, so the choice can be hers, and further treatment depends on the final results.

grid.label: Support
grid.fail: Ends without a named contact or support.
grid.pass: Introduces the breast care nurse as her named contact, with a phone number and written information.
grid.high: Asks who is at home, and offers help with telling her children.

grid.label: Checking understanding and closing
grid.fail: Closes without checking what she has understood.
grid.pass: Asks her to say what she is taking away; invites questions; confirms the next appointment.
grid.high: Offers to repeat everything with her partner present, and checks she is safe to get home.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hi. So your biopsy came back and there are some abnormal cells, a growth really.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Ms Linford: “A growth? Is it cancer?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Well, technically it's an invasive carcinoma, grade 2, ER positive. We'll probably do a wide local excision and sentinel node.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's fine, you'll be cured. So the operation will be in a few weeks.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right. The nurse will book you in. Any questions? No? Great.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors, and this is Sarah, a breast care nurse. Can I check your name and date of birth? Would you like anyone with you? What do you understand about the tests?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ms Linford: “I know they took a biopsy. I've been worried.”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm afraid the results aren't what we'd hoped. The biopsy shows breast cancer.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm so sorry. [Pause.] Take your time.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ms Linford: “Am I going to die?”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's been found early. It's small, the scan of your armpit looked normal, and we treat it with the aim of cure.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The first step is an operation: either removing the lump with a check of the lymph nodes under the arm, or removing the breast. The surgeon will go through both.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Sarah will be your main contact. Here's her number and some written information.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me what you're taking away today? Any questions? Your next appointment is with the consultant next week.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors, and this is Sarah, a breast care nurse. Can I check your name and date of birth? Would you like anyone with you? What's been going through your mind since last week? And how much detail would you like today?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Linford: “I've been terrified. Just tell me straight.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'm afraid it's not good news. The biopsy shows breast cancer. [Silence; waits for her.]

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Linford: “[Cries.] My kids are eight and eleven.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is a huge shock, and your children are the first thing on your mind. What's worrying you most?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Linford: “Am I going to die?”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's been found early: it's small and the armpit scan looked normal. We treat this with the aim of cure. It's hormone-sensitive, so tablets that block oestrogen will be part of treatment. The operation will tell us the full picture.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The first step is surgery: removing the lump, with radiotherapy afterwards, or removing the breast, with a check of the lymph nodes under the arm either way. Survival is the same with either, so there's real choice.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sarah is your named contact; here's her number. Who's at home tonight? Sarah can help with how to tell the children.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: What will you tell your partner about today? We can go over it again with him next week. Are you alright to get home?

failures.consequence: She leaves unsure whether she has cancer, and must ask someone else.

failures.move: Talking through her tears about operations.
failures.consequence: Nothing said while she is distressed is retained, and she feels unheard.
False reassurance. Staging is not complete, and trust suffers if the final histology is worse.
Pre-empts her choice between conservation and mastectomy, which have similar survival.

recovery.line: Let me be clearer: this is breast cancer.

recovery.when: You kept talking through her distress
recovery.line: I'm sorry, I've been talking a lot. Let's stop for a moment.
We treat this with the aim of cure. The operation will tell us more.

knowledge.fact: SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge (warning shot, plain words), Emotions, Strategy and summary.
Everyone with breast cancer should have a named clinical nurse specialist or key worker.
Normal axillary ultrasound: sentinel lymph node biopsy at operation.
Breast conservation with radiotherapy and mastectomy give similar survival.
ER-positive disease: adjuvant endocrine therapy. Premenopausal women choose, with the oncologist, between tamoxifen alone and ovarian suppression combinations.

recall.think: She will remember little after the word "cancer".
recall.say: "I'm afraid it's not good news. The biopsy shows breast cancer."
do: Name the nurse as her contact
recall.trap: Filling the silence with a treatment plan.
recall.finish: Named nurse, next appointment, understanding checked.

partner.opening: Ms Linford is waiting with the breast care nurse. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 42, a primary school teacher, married with two children aged 8 and 11. You found the lump in your left breast yourself. You suspect cancer but hope to be told it is a cyst. Opening: "Is it good news?" If the diagnosis is given with a warning shot and time, cry, then engage. If it is delivered abruptly or with jargon, go quiet and answer in single words. Hidden concern: your children, and how to tell them; raise it once ("My kids are eight and eleven") and say more only if asked. Ask "Am I going to die?" once you have heard the word cancer. If asked to summarise, say: "It's cancer, but early, and I'll need an operation." Your husband could not come today.

reveals.finding: "They said the biopsy would tell us. I've been dreading it."

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks what worries you most
reveals.finding: "The kids. How do I tell them?"

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks who is at home
reveals.finding: "My husband. He's at work; he couldn't get away."

push.question: Am I going to die?
push.expect: Honest and hopeful: early, small, node-negative on ultrasound, treated with the aim of cure; the operation gives final staging.

push.question: Will I lose my breast?
push.expect: Not necessarily: removing the lump with radiotherapy, or the breast, give similar survival; she will discuss the choice with the surgeon.

curveballs.prompt: "Just take the whole breast off, both of them. I want it gone."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge the fear; explain it is a decision for when she has had time and full information from the surgeon; the options will be discussed.

curveballs.prompt: "Will I need chemotherapy? Will I lose my hair?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not known yet: it depends on the results after surgery, and the oncologist will discuss it; avoid guessing.

curveballs.prompt: "Why did the GP say it was probably nothing?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge the frustration without criticising colleagues; refocus on what happens now.
